120.title: Five blessings of walking
120.hook: stamina for travel, for effort, good health, good digestion, lasting concentration
120.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners who do walking meditation sometimes walk after meals, and teachers cite the five benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya's walking discourse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turn: standing, intending, turning. Your line was the turn counts too.

Some families have a tradition: after the big dinner, everyone goes for a slow walk around the block. Nobody calls it medicine. It's just what you do. Your stomach settles, the conversation gets easier. It turns out the Buddha had his own list of reasons to walk, and one of them would make a grandmother nod. A short discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya, the numbered collection, in the book of fives, lists five blessings of walking meditation. And they're wonderfully practical.
screen: `A SLOW WALK AFTER DINNER.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT MEDICINE.` → `FIVE BLESSINGS OF WALKING.`

segments.voice: It's called the Cankama Sutta, the walking discourse, AN 5.29. One: you can endure long journeys. In the texts the Buddha and his monks travel on foot from town to town; this is stamina for that road. Two: you can endure striving. The effort of practice, the long hours of sitting, the steady work of the path all come easier to a body used to walking. Three: you're healthy. Four: what you eat and drink is well digested. That's the one the grandmother likes. Five: the concentration you gain while walking lasts a long time. That last one is worth slowing down for. The discourse simply says it lasts a long time. One way teachers explain it: concentration built while sitting perfectly still can scatter the moment you stand up, but concentration built while moving, feet lifting and placing, the body turning, is already used to movement, so it may hold up better when you get on with your day. Notice what kind of list this is. Nothing hidden or otherworldly. A teacher telling his students, in plain terms: this is good for your body, good for your practice, and good for the rest of your life. The Pali texts speak about the body in more than one way; elsewhere they ask monks to reflect on its impermanence and unattractiveness. But here it isn't something to escape or despise. It's the vehicle for the path, and walking keeps it in working order. Today's practice fits the fourth blessing exactly: a slow walk after a meal. Not for steps on a tracker. Just to let the body settle. Walking steadies.
screen: `STAMINA FOR THE ROAD.` · `STAMINA FOR THE EFFORT.` · `HEALTH, AND GOOD DIGESTION.` · `CONCENTRATION THAT LASTS.` · then, large: `WALKING STEADIES.`

segments.voice: If you can, walk slowly on your few paces of floor, a little slower than normal, feeling the whole body walking, the feet, the legs, the belly, the breath, with no labels unless you want them, as if you'd just finished a good meal and had nowhere to be. At each turn, stand for a breath. If you're seated, feel the body breathing and the feet on the floor.
Samadhi. Concentration, collectedness: the fifth blessing of walking meditation, the kind that lasts long after you stop.
Your line: walking steadies. The body is the vehicle for the path. One hundred twenty days now.

121.title: Walking in the city
121.hook: the walk to the bus can be meditation too
121.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers encourage walking practice outside the retreat lane: on the way to work, in a parking lot, at a stoplight, simply knowing the body is walking while walking at a normal pace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samadhi, the five blessings of walking: stamina, strength for effort, health, good digestion, and a concentration that lasts. Your line was walking steadies.

Tuesday, 8:12. You're late, the coffee is too hot, the bus is two blocks away and pulling in. Nobody on that sidewalk is lifting, moving and placing. There's a horn, a dog, a man on a speakerphone. All week you've had a lane: fifteen quiet steps, a slow turn, fifteen back. It's easy to think meditation lives in the lane and the city is where it goes to die. So does the walk to the bus count too? The old texts give a generous answer.
screen: `TUESDAY, 8:12, THE BUS.` → `FIFTEEN QUIET STEPS.` → `DOES THIS WALK COUNT?`

segments.voice: The lane is a training ground, not the whole game. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Buddha describes a practitioner who knows the body in every posture. When walking, they know they're walking. Standing, sitting, lying down: the same. Then the text goes further. Going out and coming back, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, eating, drinking, even using the toilet: all of it can be done with clear knowing. The word for that is sampajanna, clear comprehension: you know what you're doing while you're doing it, and why. Nothing in that list requires a quiet lane. So a city walk is a real practice, just a different one. In the lane you slow everything down. On the sidewalk you walk at a normal pace, eyes open, watching for traffic, because clear knowing includes knowing the curb is there. What you bring is the thread: the feel of the feet. Heel, sole, toes. When the mind jumps to the meeting or the argument you're rehearsing, notice it and come back to the feet. Some teachers use the city itself as the bell. Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen teacher, suggested treating a red light or a ringing phone as a small call home to the breath. You're stopped anyway; you might as well arrive. So the walk to the bus isn't wasted time between sessions. For someone with a job and kids and a commute, it may be most of the practice there's time for. The feet are always with you.
screen: `THE LANE IS TRAINING, NOT THE GAME.` · `WALKING, KNOW YOU'RE WALKING.` · `NORMAL PACE, EYES OPEN, FEET FIRST.` · `A RED LIGHT AS A BELL.` · then, large: `EVERY STEP, HERE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, feel the floor under both feet, and walk a few steps at your ordinary speed, feeling each foot land: heel, sole, toes. Stop, stand, and let the breath come and go. Then sit and picture tomorrow's first real walk, the door, the street, the corner, and pick one spot on that route, a crosswalk or a stoplight, to be your bell.
Sampajanna. Clear comprehension, knowing what you're doing while you do it: walking in the city, at a normal pace, eyes open, the feet as the thread.
Your line: every step, here. Even a red light can be a bell. Day one hundred twenty-one, complete.

122.title: Beads and hands
122.hook: the mala counts recitations on a garland of beads, often 108; mudras are the hand shapes on every Buddha statue
122.howItsDone: Many Buddhists use a mala to count mantras, the Buddha's name or the three jewels, and sit with their hands in the meditation mudra, resting in the lap with the thumbs lightly touching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sampajanna, walking in the city: the sidewalk as the lane, a red light as a bell. Your line was every step, here. Day one hundred twenty-two.

A string of wooden beads on a grandmother's wrist, clicking softly through her fingers while the news plays. The same beads, in a shop window, sold as a yoga bracelet. And on every Buddha statue you've ever passed, the hands are doing something: resting in the lap, touching the ground, raised with the palm out. None of it is random. The beads count something, and the hands are saying something. We've spent a week on the feet. Today, the hands.
screen: `BEADS ON A GRANDMOTHER'S WRIST.` → `THE SAME BEADS IN A SHOP WINDOW.` → `WHAT ARE THE HANDS SAYING?`

segments.voice: The beads are a mala. You've heard the word before: Angulimala, the finger garland. Mala means garland. A full Buddhist mala often has a hundred and eight beads, and traditions explain the number in different ways. What it's for is simple. Each bead marks one recitation, so the fingers keep count and the mind can stay with the words. In Tibetan communities that's often a mantra. In Japanese Pure Land temples, people hold their beads while saying the name of Amida Buddha. In parts of Southeast Asia, some count the qualities of the Buddha. A Chinese sutra tells of a king, worn down by war and sickness, who asks the Buddha for something simple. String a hundred and eight seeds, the Buddha tells him, and pass one through your fingers each time you recall the three jewels. If it reminds you of a rosary, that's fair: Hindus, Catholics and Muslims count prayers on beads too. Fingers are good at keeping count. Now the hands on the statues. They're called mudras, which means seals or signs. Hands resting in the lap, right on left, thumbs lightly touching: meditation. The right hand reaching down to the ground: the earth as witness, which you met on the night of the awakening. The right hand raised, palm out: do not fear. Thumb and finger making a circle at the chest: turning the wheel of the teaching. Once you know them, a statue tells you which moment of the story it's showing.

segments.voice: Sit, and rest your hands in your lap, right hand on left, palms up, thumbs lightly touching. Many Zen teachers say the thumbs are a quiet signal: pressing hard means tension, drifting apart means drowsiness. Now count the breath on your fingers, or on a mala if you have one: one breath, one finger or one bead. When you lose count, begin again at one.
Mala. A garland: a string of beads, often a hundred and eight, that counts recitations. The same word as in Angulimala. Today's word.
Your line: the hands remember. A bead or a resting hand can hold your place when the mind wanders off. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: The three refuges
123.hook: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha: the three jewels people take refuge in
123.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the three refuges, usually three times in Pali or their own language, at the start of ceremonies, at home shrines and when formally becoming a lay follower.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mala, beads and hands: a garland that counts, and hands that say rest, witness, do not fear. Your line was the hands remember. Today, a new week: the refuges and the precepts.

When things fall apart, where do you go? A person you call. A place: a kitchen, a car, a bench. A habit: the phone, the fridge, the bed at four in the afternoon. Everybody has somewhere they run to. Some of those places hold you. Some just hide you for a while. Buddhism has a word for this, and a very old answer. It's the first thing a person says when they become a Buddhist, and it's said at the start of almost every Buddhist ceremony on earth.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU RUN TO?` → `SOME PLACES HOLD YOU.` → `SOME JUST HIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Tisarana. Ti: three. Sarana: shelter, a place of safety. The three refuges, also called the three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha. The Buddha is the one who woke up, and the proof that waking up is possible for a human being. The dhamma is what he taught, and the way things actually are. The sangha is the community that practices it: in the oldest sense the monks and nuns, and more broadly everyone walking the path. The Dhammapada knows the other kind of refuge well. In Max Muller's translation: "Men, driven by fear, go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees." The verses go on to say those refuges don't end suffering, and point to the three jewels instead. Here is the formula, in Pali, unchanged for well over two thousand years. Buddham saranam gacchami. Dhammam saranam gacchami. Sangham saranam gacchami. I go to the Buddha for refuge; to the dhamma; to the sangha. It's said three times, with the words for a second time and a third time in front. A lovely detail from the early texts: the very first lay followers, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, met the Buddha just after his awakening and took refuge in only two jewels, because there was no sangha yet. The third refuge arrived when the community did. And gacchami means I go. Refuge isn't a place you sit inside; it's a direction you keep walking in. For many Buddhists, saying it is a daily beginning, not a one-time membership card.
screen: `TI-SARANA: THREE SHELTERS.` · `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `THE FIRST TWO FOLLOWERS TOOK TWO.` · `GACCHAMI: I GO.` · then, large: `THREE PLACES TO REST.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle and, if it fits who you are, say the refuges quietly, the way Buddhists say them: Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami. If you'd rather simply listen, let the three words land one at a time: someone woke up; there is a way; others walk it too. Then rest in the breath, as if you had arrived somewhere safe.
Tisarana. The three refuges: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, the three jewels Buddhists go to for shelter.
Your line: three places to rest. Some places hold you; some just hide you. See you tomorrow.

124.title: Not killing
124.hook: precept one: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life
124.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the five precepts, often right after the three refuges, at temple visits and ceremonies; the first is to refrain from taking life, and some practice it by sparing insects and, in some traditions, by eating vegetarian food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tisarana, the three refuges: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha. Your line was three places to rest.

There's a spider in the bathtub. The tissue is already in your hand. And then maybe you pause, find a glass and a postcard, and walk it out to the garden like a tiny, ungrateful guest. Why pause? It's only a spider. That pause has a place in Buddhist ethics. After the refuges come five precepts, the basic ethics of a Buddhist life, and the first one is about exactly that moment.
screen: `A SPIDER IN THE BATHTUB.` → `THE TISSUE, OR THE GLASS?` → `PRECEPT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is in Pali: Panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking life. Look at the shape of that sentence. It's a promise the person makes, in the first person, and the key word is sikkhapada: a training step. You're not claiming to be perfect; you're signing up to practice. Pana means breath, or a breathing thing, so the precept reaches past people to animals, down to the spider. The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line. In Max Muller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." That's the whole argument: everything that lives wants to go on living, just like you. Another discourse calls the five precepts great gifts. By not killing, you give every being around you freedom from fear, and you share in that safety yourself. Buddhists live this out in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly. In Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese Buddhism, monastic custom is vegetarian. In Theravada countries monks eat what they're given on the alms round, which can include meat, as long as they haven't seen, heard or suspected that the animal was killed for them. Lay Buddhists choose differently: some are vegetarian, some aren't. Where they agree is the core: don't take a life with your own intention. And the training starts small: the mosquito, the ant on the counter, the spider in the tub. Every one of them is a place to practice.
screen: `A TRAINING STEP, IN THE FIRST PERSON.` · `PANA: EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.` · `ALL TREMBLE, ALL FEAR DEATH.` · `THE GIFT OF SAFETY.` · then, large: `LET IT LIVE.`

segments.voice: Feel the breath coming in and going out: that's pana, the breath of a living thing. Think of the smallest creature you've seen today, a fly, an ant, a bird on a wire, breathing too in its own way, wanting to go on, and rest with that for a few breaths. Then, if you like, make a simple plan: the next insect you meet, you'll let it live, or carry it out.
Not killing. The first precept: a training, taken on freely, to refrain from taking the life of anything that breathes.
Your line: let it live. Every small creature wants to go on, just like you. That's day one hundred twenty-four.

125.title: Not taking
125.hook: precept two: refrain from taking what is not given
125.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the second precept, to refrain from taking what is not given, along with the other four; monks and nuns go further and accept food and other things only when they are offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, precept one, not killing: everything that breathes wants to go on. Your line was let it live.

Quick inventory. Is there a book on your shelf that belongs to someone else? A casserole dish from a neighbor, a hoodie from an ex, a charger from work that somehow came home? Nobody here is a burglar. But it's easy to end up holding something that was never quite given. The second precept sounds like it's about thieves. Listen to how it's actually worded, though, and it gets much closer to home.
screen: `A BORROWED BOOK. A NEIGHBOR'S DISH.` → `NOBODY HERE IS A BURGLAR.` → `PRECEPT TWO.`

segments.voice: In Pali: Adinnadana veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking what is not given. Adinna: not given. Adana: taking. Notice it doesn't say don't steal. It says don't take what isn't given, and that's a wider door. Stealing is only the loud version. The quiet versions are everywhere: the book you meant to return, the extra change the cashier handed you by mistake, the credit for a colleague's idea, the hour of someone's time you took without asking. Each time, the question is the same: was this freely handed to me, or did I just take it? The early discourses describe someone who keeps this precept as one who doesn't take, in the village or in the forest, what belongs to someone else. The rule for monks and nuns is stricter still: apart from water and a tooth-cleaning stick, they may not eat anything unless it's been offered. A monk won't pick an apple off a table until someone hands it to him. You'll see that again next week, on the alms round. The flip side of not taking is generosity, and that's where next week goes. A person trained in only what's given lives with a certain lightness. Nobody's looking for them. Nothing in the house is a small, guilty weight. What you have, you really have, because it was given. Some teachers today widen the precept further, to time, to attention, to credit. The old wording holds all of it.

segments.voice: Take a slow walk, in your mind, through your home: the shelves, the kitchen, the closet, the desk drawer. Is there anything there that was lent to you and never went back? Just notice it without judging, picture yourself handing it back and the other person's face, then return to the breath, which nobody lent you.
Not taking. The second precept: a training to take only what is freely given, which reaches much further than stealing.
Your line: only what's given. Stealing is only the loud version. Day one hundred twenty-five, done.

126.title: Sexual conduct
126.hook: precept three: refrain from sexual misconduct; harm, not shame, is the measure
126.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists recite the third precept with the other four; communities interpret its details differently, and monks and nuns keep full celibacy under their monastic rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, precept two, not taking: the borrowed book, the extra change. Your line was only what's given.

Of the five precepts, this is the one a listener might brace for: a list of forbidden things, a raised eyebrow, the feeling of being judged before a word is said. But the way teachers explain it today, shame isn't its measure. It asks the same question the first two precepts asked about life and about things: is anyone being harmed?
screen: `BRACING FOR THE LIST.` → `NOT SHAME.` → `IS ANYONE HARMED?`

segments.voice: In Pali: Kamesu micchacara veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from misconduct in sensual pleasures. Kama means sensual pleasure, desire. Micchacara means wrong conduct, literally going the wrong way. The precept doesn't name desire itself. Lay Buddhists marry, fall in love, raise families, and the texts treat that as a normal human life. It names going the wrong way with desire. The early discourses make that concrete: someone who keeps this precept doesn't get involved with people who are under someone else's protection, or promised to someone else. In the world those texts came from, that meant a daughter in her family's care, or a wife or a betrothed woman. Teachers today read one thread through that list: harm, to the other person, to a partner who trusted you, to families. So they often put it in a single line: harm, not shame, is the measure. Honesty, consent, keeping the promises you've made, not using another person. Buddhist communities read the details in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly. More traditional communities keep closely to the old lists. Other teachers, especially in newer communities, focus on the principle of not causing harm and apply it to every kind of relationship. Monks and nuns go further still: they keep complete celibacy. What they all share is the heart of it. Desire is human. What you do with it can heal or wound. The precept is a training in the first.

Then, if you like, send them the old wish from the metta weeks: may you be safe, may you be at ease.
Sexual conduct. The third precept: a training not to go the wrong way with desire, where the measure is harm, not shame.
